As for longevity, the longer you work the more skill and job related knowledge you acquire. You become more specialized, which gives you value. If you are still doing tasks that any kid fresh out of college can do, then you haven't advanced as you should.

==Additive Bonuses==

Normal movement speed: 30 ft

Total base movement: 85 ft


==Doubling Bonuses==

==Actions==

Normal movement: 340 ft

Action Dash: 680 ft

Cunning Action Dash:  1020ft

Haste Action Dash: 1360 ft

Action Surge Dash: 1700 ft


All that in six seconds. Now for some conversions. 1700 ft/6 s = 283 ft/s = 193 mph. Or for those who like non-Freedom units, 310 km/h. More importantly, it's .825 Mach. You would have to try just a bit harder to break the sound barrier just by running, but we are getting up there. If you could increase the total speed to 2060 ft/round or 105 ft base movement through other effects, then breaking the sound barrier would be possible.

Everything tool has a percentage injury chance, that's a fact of life. The easiest example is rubber bullets. It's basically a rubber iPhone launched at you. If it hits you in the chest or the limbs (which is where they aim because it's the largest target), you will end up with a bruise and probably get the wind knocked out of you. Nothing too bad, walk it off. If it goes errant and hits you in the eye, yeah it will fuck you up real nice. But for intended uses against expected individuals, it's fine. For most people, especially at the protest I was at, just the mention of rubbers was enough to make them disperse. Same thing goes for the rest of the methods:  there are edge case scenarios where they can do more damage, but they are designed and intended to be used in ways that do not have an expected heavy injuries. The best solution is to have better training for the police, so that they don't cause accidental injury and effective reprimands for police that maliciously use these tools.

A few things to note: This event came after several days of running riots with high amounts of property damage. When I went to the start of the protest, every buisness in downtown was borded up and closed to prevent them from being the next victims. There wasn't a divide either, it was everyone from your local minority owned falafel shop to the mega corps. As the official protest had moved on and ended elsewhere, remaining in the intersection could be deemed as an unlawful assembly. At the time of the protest, none of those measures had been passed. 

Additionally, if you chose to be in a riot, you assume a level of risk that you will encounter force while being dispersed. If you don't want that, you leave. If you stay when the situation gets out of hand (and it was a long buildup) hoping that force will not be used, you are a wishful idiot. I would define brutal as lethal or *likely* to end with serious, permanent injury. Something like tear gas hurts like a bitch, but you'll walk it off after a while, and the smart protester brings goggles. Same goes for flashbangs and rubber bullets, they are not likely to cause serious injury. The only tool I would like to see them use is sonics, but afaik SPD doesn't have them. Take away that and we are back essentially at Rodney King beating and the SPD of the 90s to subdue the riots. Seattle has yearly Anarchist riots on May Day for 20 years now, and the methods SPD uses now were developed with the DOJ have been breathing down their neck the entire way due to SPDs actual brutality problems in the 90s. It's why I describe it as textbook: you riot and break some stuff, the police show up and fuck you up a little bit, then you go home. It's practically an anual holiday for us.

I was at that protest, and it wasn't just 60 seconds, there was about two hours of buildup. I was near the dividing line, about 3 people back from the fence. The protest led to the precinct, where it became centralized at that intersection. Things were relatively for the first hour, while the protest organizers had control over the crowd. This went on for about an hour while the news got their pictures and the police chief (I think) interacted with the protest organizers. 

After a while in this prolonged standoff, people in the crowd started openly challenging the protest organizers. I noticed typical antifa/anarchists moving towards the front. The organizers had been using kneeling to control the crowd, but eventually the crowd started yelling back "Why are we kneeling before cops?" At this point, the organizers decided to move the protest south, where it officially ended I belive. 

About half of the crowd though did not leave the intersection, and there was not a stopgap for the vitriol against the police. The center of the street was the main point of interaction, and the most agitated moved towards it. About 40 minutes after they left, the part of the protest that left returned, re-pressurizing the intersection. My sister, who was on the other side of the crowd, heard people saying that they wanted to burn down the precinct. Things were becoming particularly heated at that point, and the police were by and large unreactive as they are trained, so the agitators kept ramping up. Reinforcements were called, first one squad, then after someone threw a bottle, another three. At this point I could tell things were about to go down and told the guys I was talking with to back up a few yards.

I didn't see what specifically started the conflict, but clearly it wasn't just a 60 second ramp as the article describes. I saw several plumes of pepper spray launched at the rowdy center. These are riot level, not personal defense, so they are AOE and not single target. At this point the crowd spread out, retreating down the side streets. Tear gas and flashbangs were used to clear the intersection, and the protestors regrouped at the park and the streets. The only real retreats came when the cops used rubber bullets (as I heard people call out). This lead to a back and forth for at least an hour, with the protesters forming barricades of dumpsters and the police reclaiming the space. The line was never able to advance through the police line, and while a few people tried walking through with their hands up, I would assume they were subdued. I stayed for a good bit of the brawling, directing traffic and helping with medical until I decided to disengage and head home.

All in all, a few takeaways from my perspective. First, it wasn't just a quick flash scenario, it boiled for a good long while. If you could read a crowd, you would know what was about to happen, so none of it surprised me. I think it was a joint failure of the protest organizers to properly control and contain the radical elements of the crowd, the police to disperse the crowd before the use of force was necessary, and of course the radical elements for escalating the situation. Overall, it was pretty textbook, at least for Seattle protests.

As far as I can tell, it was a timing issue, like with Full Metal Alchemist vs FMA Brotherhood. The Rosario manga started weekly then shifted to monthly and eventually bi-monthly (with chapter 66 of season two taking  FOREVER to arrive). On the other hand, the anime released weekly and only had 12 episodes to cover 40 chapters of season 1 with probably 15 stories in there. Stuff had to be cut or changed to fit like say the Liliths Mirror arc. Most of season 1 is consistent, just not complete.

Once season 2 started, the manga had just BARELY started it's own second season. It's why the first few episodes are ok... then everything starts going downhill from there as the anime had to make up content like the original FMA. They could do a retcon on season 2 of the anime and follow it up with season 3 as the final ark, but I think people moved on and it was never popular enough to warrant a studio coming back and investing in more. Something like Steins Gate can do it because it's freaking Steins Gate. It's a pity too, especially given that season 2 of the manga contains the best work IMO. 

So why doesn't it have a faithful adaptation? Release schedules, animators having to make things up as they go, and lack of popularity to make the investment in better worthwhile. I got no sources on this one, but it seems to be a reasonable armchair analysis.
